pos: interjection (the sixth word from the cross)
etymology: From the Lord's cry on the cross (John 19:30), rendering the Greek tetelestai, “it has been accomplished, completed, paid in full.”
biblical_def: “It is finished” is the great cry of the Lord Jesus from the cross, the sixth of His seven words, rendering the Greek tetelestai—“it has been accomplished, completed, brought to its appointed end.” It was no gasp of defeat but a shout of triumph: the work of redemption was done. The word tetelestai was used in the commerce of the day stamped upon a settled account—“paid in full”—and upon the cross the debt of His people's sin was paid to the last farthing. The dictionary marks “It is finished” as the death-knell of every gospel of human merit and the charter of the believer's assurance. By that one offering Christ hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified; by His own blood He entered once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption; and the handwriting of ordinances that was against us He blotted out, nailing it to His cross. Nothing remains to be added. The atonement is complete, the law satisfied, the wrath exhausted, the curse borne, the price paid—all finished. The dictionary holds the word against the perennial error that would add the sinner's works, penances, or merits to the finished work of Christ. To say “it is finished” is to say there is nothing left for the sinner to finish; salvation is not Christ's work begun and the sinner's work completing it, but Christ's work alone, accomplished. The Roman Mass that re-presents the sacrifice, the legalism that pays its own debt, and the anxious soul that strives to add to the cross all deny the cry of Calvary. The believer rests where Christ rested His head: the work is done, the account is settled, it is finished.
webster_summary: The Lord's triumphant cry from the cross (John 19:30, tetelestai, “paid in full”); the work of redemption complete and the debt of sin discharged—the death-knell of every gospel of human merit and the charter of the believer's assurance.
webster_full: IT IS FINISHED, interjection. [Greek tetelestai, “it is accomplished, paid in full.”] The Lord's sixth word from the cross.
“He said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost” (John 19:30).
Not a gasp of defeat but a shout of triumph: the work of redemption done.
By one offering He hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified (Hebrews 10:14).
The death-knell of every gospel of human merit; nothing remains to be added.
scriptures: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.
Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;
corruption_summary: The cry is denied by the Roman Mass that re-presents the sacrifice, the legalism that pays its own debt, and the anxious striving that would add works to the finished work of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: “It is finished” is itself the answer to the corruption of adding to Christ's work. The cry declares the atonement complete: the debt paid in full, the law satisfied, the wrath exhausted, the curse borne. Every scheme that would add the sinner's works, penances, or merits to that finished work denies the word of Calvary. The Roman Mass, which claims to re-present the one sacrifice again and again, contradicts the once-for-all by which Christ perfected His people; the legalist who pays his own debt insults the payment already made; and the anxious soul striving to finish what Christ finished labours against the cross.

The dictionary holds the comfort the word secures. To say “it is finished” is to say there is nothing left for the sinner to finish. Salvation is not Christ's work begun and the believer's work completing it, but Christ's work alone, accomplished and accepted, the account stamped “paid in full.” The believer rests where the Saviour bowed His head—in a finished redemption—and draws his assurance not from his own striving but from the cry of the cross. The work is done; the price is paid; the soul that trusts the finished work of Christ may cease from its own works and rest, for it is finished.
roots_summary: From the Greek tetelestai (perfect tense of teleo, to finish, complete, accomplish), a commercial term stamped “paid in full” on a settled account.
roots_lines: Tetelestai, Greek, “it has been finished, accomplished, completed.”
From teleo, to bring to an end, to fulfil, to pay.
A commercial term stamped “paid in full” on a discharged debt.
The sixth of the seven words from the cross (John 19:30).
A cry of triumph, not defeat: the work of redemption accomplished.
usage: The pastor preached “it is finished” to show the debt of sin paid in full at the cross.
He answered the Mass: Christ perfected His people by one offering, never to be repeated.
She rested her assurance on the finished work, ceasing from striving to add to the cross.

etymology: From the Authorized Version of Hebrews 9:14, the blood of Christ that purges the conscience from dead works; the cleansing of the inner moral judgment by the once-for-all sacrifice.
biblical_def: To cleanse the conscience is the work of the blood of Christ that purges the believer's inner moral judgment from the guilt of sin and from dead works, that he may serve the living God with freedom and assurance. The writer to the Hebrews sets it against the old sacrifices, which could sanctify outwardly but never reach the conscience: “How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?” The conscience—the inner witness that accuses or excuses—is defiled by sin and burdened with guilt, and no ceremony, penance, or human work can wash it clean; only the blood of Christ, applied by faith, sprinkles the heart from an evil conscience. So the believer is bidden to draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having his heart sprinkled from an evil conscience; and the answer of a good conscience toward God is given by the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The dictionary marks the cleansing of the conscience as a chief benefit of the finished work and the ground of the believer's peace with God. It holds the doctrine against two errors. The first is the Roman system of penance and works, which seeks to relieve the guilty conscience by human satisfactions that can never reach it. The second is the modern therapeutic counterfeit, which would quiet the conscience not by cleansing guilt but by denying it—reframing sin as mere brokenness and silencing the accusing witness rather than washing it. The dictionary holds that the conscience is cleansed, not silenced: real guilt is really purged by real blood, that the believer may serve the living God with a heart at peace.
webster_summary: The work of the blood of Christ that purges the inner moral judgment from guilt and dead works (Hebrews 9:14), giving full assurance to serve the living God; against Roman penance that cannot reach it and therapeutic counterfeits that deny guilt rather than cleanse it.
webster_full: CLEANSE THE CONSCIENCE, verb phrase. The purging of the inner moral judgment by the blood of Christ.
“The blood of Christ… purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14).
The old sacrifices could not reach the conscience; the blood of Christ does.
Draw near with hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience (Hebrews 10:22).
The conscience is cleansed of real guilt, not merely silenced.
scriptures: How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:
Now the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned:
corruption_summary: Roman penance seeks to relieve the guilty conscience by works that cannot reach it; the therapeutic counterfeit quiets the conscience by denying guilt rather than cleansing it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the conscience is cleansed of real guilt by real blood. The first corruption is the Roman system of penance and human satisfactions, which seeks to relieve the burdened conscience by works, indulgences, and ceremonies that, like the old sacrifices, can never reach it. The writer to the Hebrews is emphatic: the blood of bulls and goats could sanctify outwardly but not purge the conscience; only the blood of Christ does. To send the guilty soul to its own works for relief is to leave the conscience uncleansed.

The opposite and more modern corruption is the therapeutic counterfeit, which would quiet the conscience not by cleansing guilt but by denying it—relabelling sin as brokenness or woundedness, and silencing the accusing witness rather than washing it. But a conscience merely silenced is not a conscience cleansed; the guilt remains though the alarm is muted. The dictionary holds the gospel cure: the conscience is purged, not numbed. Real guilt is really removed by the blood of Christ applied by faith, so that the believer draws near in full assurance, his heart sprinkled from an evil conscience, free at last to serve the living God with a peace the world's techniques can never give.
roots_summary: From “conscience” (Latin conscientia, joint-knowledge) and the Greek katharizo (to purge, cleanse); the inner moral witness purged from dead works by the blood of Christ.
roots_lines: Syneidesis, Greek, conscience, the inner witness that accuses or excuses.
Katharizo, Greek, to cleanse or purge, of the conscience purged by Christ's blood.
“Dead works,” the works of a guilty, unregenerate heart, from which it is cleansed.
Set against the old sacrifices, which could not reach the conscience.
The “answer of a good conscience” secured by the resurrection (1 Peter 3:21).
usage: The pastor preached the cleansed conscience to the guilt-burdened soul, pointing to the blood of Christ.
He answered Roman penance: no human work can reach the conscience that Christ's blood purges.
She found peace not by silencing guilt but by having it cleansed, drawing near in full assurance.

etymology: From “works” and “righteousness”; the error of seeking to be justified before God by one's own works or moral effort rather than by the imputed righteousness of Christ received through faith.
biblical_def: Works-righteousness is the error of seeking to be justified before God by one's own works, merit, or moral effort, rather than by the imputed righteousness of Christ received through faith alone. It is the native religion of the fallen heart, the instinct that supposes a man may commend himself to God by his doing—and it is the great error the gospel overthrows. Scripture is decisive: “by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin”; salvation is “not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy”; “not of works, lest any man should boast.” And the prophet strips away the sinner's last refuge: “all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.” The dictionary marks works-righteousness as the perennial enemy of the gospel of grace, appearing under many names. It is the Judaizing that adds the law to Christ; it is the Roman system of merit, penance, and works anathematized at Trent; it is the moralism that trusts in being a good person; and it is the subtle religion of the church-going man who, while professing grace, secretly rests on his own performance. The dictionary holds against it the doctrine of justification by faith alone: the sinner is accepted not for any righteousness of his own—for he has none that is not as filthy rags—but for the perfect righteousness of Christ, imputed to him and received by the empty hand of faith. Good works are the necessary fruit of faith, but never its ground; they follow justification as its evidence, and can never be its cause. To trust in works is to forsake Christ; to rest in Christ is to be done with works as a ground of acceptance and free at last to do them out of love.
webster_summary: The error of seeking justification before God by one's own works rather than by Christ's imputed righteousness received through faith (Romans 3:20; Titus 3:5); the native religion of the fallen heart and the perennial enemy of the gospel of grace.
webster_full: WORKS-RIGHTEOUSNESS, noun. Seeking justification by one's own works rather than Christ's imputed righteousness.
“By the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified” (Romans 3:20).
Salvation is not by works of righteousness we have done, but by mercy (Titus 3:5).
“Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Ephesians 2:9).
Our own righteousnesses are as filthy rags (Isaiah 64:6).
scriptures: Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin.
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away.
corruption_summary: Works-righteousness is itself the corruption: the native religion of the fallen heart, appearing as Judaizing, Roman merit, moralism, and the secret self-trust of the professing believer.
corruption_paragraphs: Works-righteousness is the corruption itself—the perennial enemy of the gospel and the native religion of the fallen heart. It supposes a man may commend himself to God by his own doing, and it appears under many names: the Judaizing that adds the law to Christ, the Roman system of merit and penance anathematized at Trent, the moralism that trusts in being a decent person, and, most subtly, the secret self-reliance of the church-going man who professes grace with his lips while resting on his performance in his heart. Scripture demolishes it: no flesh is justified by the deeds of the law, salvation is not by works but by mercy, and our best righteousnesses are filthy rags.

The dictionary holds against it the doctrine of justification by faith alone. The sinner is accepted not for any righteousness of his own—he has none that is not as filthy rags—but for the perfect righteousness of Christ, imputed to him and received by the empty hand of faith. The dictionary marks the crucial place of good works lest the answer be mistaken for antinomianism: good works are the necessary fruit and evidence of justifying faith, but never its ground. They follow acceptance; they cannot cause it. To trust in works is to forsake Christ and to fall from grace; to rest in Christ alone is to be done with works as a ground of acceptance, and so set free to do them gladly out of love, not fear.
roots_summary: From “works” (the deeds of the law) and “righteousness”; the seeking of a justifying righteousness from one's own doing, against the imputed righteousness of Christ received by faith.
roots_lines: “Works of the law” (Greek erga nomou), by which no flesh is justified (Romans 3:20).
Dikaiosune, Greek, righteousness, sought wrongly from one's own doing.
“Filthy rags” (Hebrew beged 'iddim), the value of self-righteousness (Isaiah 64:6).
The native religion of the fallen heart, the opposite of sola fide.
Good works the fruit and evidence of faith, never its ground.
usage: The pastor preached against works-righteousness, the secret self-trust even of professing believers.
He held justification by faith alone: Christ's righteousness imputed, not our filthy rags.
She rested in Christ alone, freed to do good works out of love, not as a ground of acceptance.

etymology: The ninth chapter of the prophecy of Isaiah, containing the great messianic promise of the child born and the son given, whose name is Wonderful, Counsellor, the mighty God.
biblical_def: Isaiah 9 is the chapter of the prophecy of Isaiah containing one of the greatest of all messianic promises: the child born and the son given, on whose shoulder the government rests, and whose name is called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. Spoken into the darkness of the Assyrian crisis, when the land lay under the shadow of death, the prophecy promises a great light to the people that walked in darkness, dawning in the region of Galilee that the gospel records as fulfilled when Christ began His ministry there. The dictionary marks Isaiah 9 as a chief proof of the deity, the kingship, and the eternal reign of the promised Messiah. The titles are not mere honorifics but divine names: He who is born a child is “the mighty God” (El Gibbor) and “the everlasting Father”—not the Father of the Trinity, but the Father of eternity, the everlasting One, the Author of the age to come—the Prince whose peace and government shall have no end, established upon the throne of David for ever by the zeal of the LORD of hosts. The dictionary holds the chapter against the historical-critical reading that would confine the prophecy to an earthly Judahite king (Hezekiah or another), denying its reference to Christ and explaining away the divine titles. The titles are too high for any mere man: no earthly king is the mighty God or reigns for ever. Isaiah 9 prophesies the incarnate Son, born in Bethlehem, who dawned as light in Galilee of the Gentiles and reigns now on the throne of His father David, of whose increase and peace there shall be no end. It is read at the church's celebration of the incarnation, for in it the prophet, seven centuries before, named the child who is the mighty God.
webster_summary: The chapter of Isaiah's great messianic promise—the child born, the son given, named Wonderful, Counsellor, the mighty God, the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6-7); a chief proof of the deity and eternal kingship of Christ, fulfilled as light in Galilee.
webster_full: ISAIAH 9, proper noun. The chapter of Isaiah's great messianic promise of the child born and the son given.
“The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2).
“Unto us a child is born… The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).
Of the increase of His government there shall be no end (Isaiah 9:7).
Fulfilled as light dawning in Galilee at Christ's ministry (Matthew 4:16).
scriptures: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.

Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will perform this.
The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.
corruption_summary: The historical-critical reading confines the prophecy to an earthly Judahite king (Hezekiah), denying its reference to Christ and explaining away the divine titles too high for any mere man.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the messianic and divine reference of the prophecy. The historical-critical school confines Isaiah 9 to an earthly Judahite king—Hezekiah or another—and explains away the divine titles as oriental court flattery, denying that the chapter speaks of Christ. The dictionary rejects this on the testimony of the New Testament, which sees the prophecy fulfilled when the light dawned in Galilee at Christ's ministry, and on the titles themselves, which are too high for any mere man. No earthly king is “the mighty God” or reigns for ever; the child born is the incarnate Son.

The dictionary holds the full weight of the titles. He who is born a child is named El Gibbor, the mighty God, and the everlasting Father—not a confusion with the First Person of the Trinity, but the Father of eternity, the everlasting One, the author of the age to come. He is the Prince of Peace whose government and peace shall have no end, established on the throne of David for ever by the zeal of the LORD of hosts. The dictionary reads Isaiah 9, with the church of every age, as a prophecy of the incarnate Christ—born in Bethlehem, dawning as light in Galilee of the Gentiles, reigning now on David's throne—the chapter in which the prophet, seven centuries before the manger, named the child who is the mighty God.
roots_summary: The ninth chapter of Isaiah; its great verse (9:6) heaps four (or five) throne-names upon the messianic child, including El Gibbor (“the mighty God”) and Sar-Shalom (“Prince of Peace”).
roots_lines: Isaiah 9, spoken into the darkness of the Assyrian crisis.

Avi-'ad, “everlasting Father,” the Father of eternity.
Sar-Shalom, Hebrew, “Prince of Peace.”
Fulfilled as light in “Galilee of the Gentiles” (Matthew 4:15-16).
usage: The pastor preached Isaiah 9 at the incarnation: the child born is named the mighty God.
He answered the critic that no earthly king is the mighty God or reigns for ever.
She read the light dawning in Galilee as the fulfilment of the prophet's word.

etymology: From Ezekiel 14:3, “these men have set up their idols in their heart”; the inward idol—any desire, person, or thing loved, trusted, or served in the place of God.
biblical_def: An idol of the heart is an inward idol—any desire, person, possession, or pursuit that a man loves, trusts, fears, or serves in the place of God, even where no outward image is bowed to. The phrase comes from Ezekiel, where the LORD says of the elders who came to inquire of Him, “these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumblingblock of their iniquity before their face,” and calls them to “repent, and turn yourselves from your idols.” The dictionary marks the idol of the heart as the root and inward form of all idolatry, of which carved images are only the outward expression. The apostle names covetousness idolatry, for the covetous man sets his heart on riches as his god; and John closes his epistle, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols”—not statues, but the rival loves of the heart. Anything loved more than God, trusted more than God, feared more than God, or served before God is an idol of the heart: money, reputation, pleasure, comfort, family, self, even ministry or doctrine held as an end in itself. Calvin rightly called the human heart a perpetual factory of idols, ever forging new gods to set in the place of the true. The dictionary holds the doctrine against the modern blindness that thinks idolatry an ancient sin of statues, irrelevant to the sophisticated. The heart's idolatry is the most common and the most hidden of sins, and the most modern: the man who would never bow to an image bows daily to the gods of his own desire. The remedy is not mere outward reform but the repentance Ezekiel commands—turning from the idols of the heart to the living God—and the renewing of the heart of flesh, that the affections may be set on God above all.
webster_summary: An inward idol—anything loved, trusted, feared, or served in the place of God (Ezekiel 14:3); the root and hidden form of all idolatry (covetousness is idolatry), the heart being, as Calvin said, a perpetual factory of idols.
webster_full: IDOL OF THE HEART, noun phrase. An inward idol loved, trusted, or served in the place of God.
“These men have set up their idols in their heart” (Ezekiel 14:3).
The root of all idolatry, of which carved images are the outward form.
Covetousness is idolatry (Colossians 3:5); “keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).
Calvin: the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols.
scriptures: Son of man, these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumblingblock of their iniquity before their face: should I be enquired of at all by them?
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.
Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Repent, and turn yourselves from your idols; and turn away your faces from all your abominations.
corruption_summary: The modern blindness thinks idolatry an ancient sin of statues, irrelevant to the sophisticated; but the heart's idolatry is the most common, hidden, and modern of sins.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that idolatry is first and chiefly a sin of the heart. The modern reader supposes idolatry an ancient and primitive matter of statues, irrelevant to a sophisticated age that bows to no carved image. The dictionary answers from Ezekiel and the apostles: the idol is first set up in the heart, and the carved image is only its outward expression. The man who would never bow to a statue bows daily to the gods of his own desire—money, reputation, pleasure, comfort, family, self—loving, trusting, fearing, and serving the creature in the place of the Creator.

Calvin rightly named the human heart a perpetual factory of idols, ever forging new gods to set in the place of the true. The dictionary holds that the heart's idolatry is the most common of sins and the most hidden, often dressed in respectable or even religious clothing—ministry, doctrine, or family held as ends in themselves can become idols. The remedy is not mere outward reform but the repentance Ezekiel commands: turn from the idols of the heart to the living God. The Spirit who gives the heart of flesh re-orders its affections, dethroning the rival loves and setting God above all—for the first commandment reaches not the hands only but the heart, which is to have no other gods before Him.
roots_summary: From Ezekiel 14:3, the idols (Hebrew gillulim) “set up in the heart”; the inward idolatry of the affections, of which covetousness is the New Testament example.
roots_lines: Gillulim, Hebrew, idols (a term of contempt), set up “in the heart” (Ezekiel 14:3).
The inward root of all idolatry, prior to any outward image.
Covetousness named idolatry (Colossians 3:5)—the heart's rival god.
“Keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21)—the heart's rival loves.
Calvin's “perpetual factory of idols” (fabrica idolorum).
usage: The pastor preached the idol of the heart, that the man who bows to no statue bows to his desires.
He named covetousness idolatry, the heart setting riches in the place of God.
She repented of the idols of her heart, turning her affections to the living God.

etymology: From “mother” (Old English modor) and “-hood” (state or condition); the God-given calling and honour of the mother in the bearing, nurture, and instruction of children.
biblical_def: Motherhood is the God-given calling and honour of the mother in the bearing, nurture, and instruction of her children—a high and holy vocation woven into the creation order and exalted throughout Scripture. The bearing of children is named a blessing, not a burden: “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.” The mother's labour is honoured: the virtuous woman's children arise up and call her blessed; the aged women are to teach the young women to love their husbands and to love their children; and the apostle says, in a much-discussed verse, that the woman “shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety”—the godly mother walking out her calling in faith. The dictionary marks motherhood as a chief and honourable sphere of a woman's service to God, against the spirit of the age. The first corruption is the feminist devaluing of motherhood, which treats childbearing and the nurture of children as a lesser, even oppressive, role to be escaped for the “real” fulfilment of career and self—despising the heritage of the LORD and the calling He honours. The dictionary names this a corruption of the creation design, in which the woman's glory in the home and in the raising of children is no demeaning but a dignity. The opposite error is the sentimentality that idolizes motherhood as a woman's only worth or makes it an idol, forgetting that her first calling is to fear and love God, of which faithful motherhood is one expression. The dictionary holds the biblical honour: motherhood is a holy vocation, the fruit of the womb a reward of God, the godly mother a builder of the house and a shaper of generations, who labours not for the praise of men but in faith, charity, and holiness before God.
webster_summary: The God-given calling and honour of the mother in bearing, nurturing, and instructing children (Psalm 127:3; Titus 2:4); a holy vocation, against the feminist devaluing of motherhood and the sentimentality that idolizes it.
webster_full: MOTHERHOOD, noun. [Old English modor.] The God-given calling of the mother in bearing and nurturing children.
Children are an heritage of the LORD, the fruit of the womb His reward (Psalm 127:3).
Her children arise up and call her blessed (Proverbs 31:28).
The aged women teach the young to love their children (Titus 2:4).
A holy vocation, against the devaluing of motherhood and its idolizing.
scriptures: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,
Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety.
corruption_summary: Feminism devalues motherhood as a lesser, oppressive role to be escaped for career and self; the opposite sentimentality idolizes it as a woman's only worth. Both miss the holy vocation Scripture honours.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of motherhood as a holy calling. The chief corruption of the age is the feminist devaluing of motherhood, which treats childbearing and the nurture of children as a lesser, confining, even oppressive role to be escaped for the “real” fulfilment of career and self-realization. The dictionary names this a corruption of the creation design and a contempt for what God calls a blessing: children are the heritage of the LORD and the fruit of the womb His reward, and the mother who bears and raises them in faith fills a vocation God Himself honours. Her glory in the home is no demeaning but a dignity.

The opposite error is a sentimentality that idolizes motherhood—making it a woman's only worth, or an idol of the heart, so that the childless or the single woman is counted a failure and the mother's identity rests wholly in her children rather than in God. The dictionary holds the biblical balance: motherhood is a high and honourable calling, but a woman's first calling is to fear and love God, of which faithful motherhood is one blessed expression. The godly mother labours not for the praise of men nor for her own fulfilment as an end, but in faith, charity, and holiness before God—a builder of the house, a shaper of generations, blessed by her children and praised in the gates.
roots_summary: From the Old English modor (mother) and “-hood” (state or condition); the calling and honour of the mother, grounded in the creation blessing of fruitfulness.
roots_lines: Modor, Old English, mother, with “-hood,” the state or condition.
Grounded in the creation blessing: be fruitful and multiply (Genesis 1:28).
The fruit of the womb a “reward” (Hebrew sakar) of the LORD (Psalm 127:3).
The godly mother's children “call her blessed” (Proverbs 31:28).
A holy vocation within the complementary order of creation.
usage: The pastor honoured motherhood as a holy calling against the spirit that devalues it.

She raised her children in faith, charity, and holiness, blessed in her high vocation.

etymology: From “work” and “vocation” (Latin vocatio, a calling); the doctrine that honest labour is a God-given calling, to be done heartily as unto the Lord.
biblical_def: Work and vocation name the doctrine that honest labour is a God-given calling, instituted at creation and to be done heartily as unto the Lord. Work is not a result of the fall but a creation ordinance: before sin entered, “the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.” The fall brought toil, sweat, and thorns, but did not make labour itself a curse; work remains a creational good and a calling. The apostle dignifies all lawful labour by directing it to God: “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men”; and he lays down the plain rule against idleness, “that if any would not work, neither should he eat,” and bids every man “abide in the same calling wherein he was called.” The dictionary marks the doctrine of vocation as the Reformation's great recovery against the medieval notion that only the priest, monk, and nun had a “calling,” while ordinary labour was a lower, secular thing. The Reformers taught that the farmer, the mother, the merchant, and the magistrate serve God in their callings as truly as the minister—that there is no sacred-secular divide, and that the milkmaid milking her cow to the glory of God does a work as holy as the preacher in his pulpit. The dictionary holds this against two errors: the false spirituality that despises ordinary work as unspiritual, and the modern idolatry of work that makes career the source of identity and worth, the idol of the heart before which the age bows. True vocation is neither despised nor idolized: it is honest labour received as a calling from God, done diligently and heartily to His glory, balanced by the Sabbath rest He appointed, and held as service to God and neighbour, not as the ground of one's worth.
webster_summary: The doctrine that honest labour is a God-given calling, instituted at creation and done heartily as unto the Lord (Genesis 2:15; Colossians 3:23); the Reformation's recovery against the sacred-secular divide, against both despising work and idolizing career.

corruption_summary: One error is the false spirituality that despises ordinary work as unspiritual; the other is the modern idolatry of work that makes career the source of identity and worth—the idol of the heart of the age.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of honest labour as a calling from God. The first corruption is the false spirituality, ancient and modern, that despises ordinary work as unspiritual—ranking the “sacred” callings of ministry above the “secular” labour of the farmer, the mother, and the merchant. The Reformation recovered the truth against this: there is no sacred-secular divide in callings; the believer serves God in his lawful work as truly as the minister in his, and the humblest labour done heartily to the Lord is holy. Work is a creation ordinance, given before the fall, a good and dignified service to God and neighbour.

The opposite and more modern corruption is the idolatry of work—making career the source of identity, meaning, and worth, the idol of the heart before which the age bows. The man who finds his whole self in his work has made a god of it, and when the work fails he is undone. The dictionary holds the balance: work is neither to be despised nor idolized. It is honest labour received as a calling from God, done diligently and heartily to His glory, balanced by the Sabbath rest He appointed, and held as service rendered to God and neighbour—never as the ground of one's worth, which rests in being made in God's image and, for the believer, redeemed by Christ.

etymology: From “private” (Latin privatus, one's own) and “property” (Latin proprietas, ownership); the lawful right of ownership, grounded in the eighth commandment.
biblical_def: Private property is the lawful right of a man to own, possess, and dispose of his goods, a right grounded in the moral law of God and presupposed by the eighth commandment, “Thou shalt not steal.” The very command against theft assumes that men rightly own what is theirs; one cannot steal what no one owns. Scripture everywhere honours lawful ownership and the inheritance handed down: the boundary-stones of the fathers are not to be removed; Naboth would not sell the inheritance of his fathers, and Ahab's seizure of his vineyard by murder is recorded as a great wickedness; and Peter affirmed to Ananias that his property, while it remained and after it was sold, was his own and in his own power—his sin was not in owning but in lying. The dictionary marks private property as a creational and moral good, against two opposite corruptions. The first is collectivism—the socialist and communist denial of private property, which abolishes ownership in the name of equality, violating the eighth commandment on a national scale and breeding tyranny, for the state that owns all owns the men who depend on it. The voluntary sharing of the early church in Acts was just that—voluntary, the goods remaining the owners' to give—not a compelled communism. The second corruption is the greed and idolatry of possessions that, while affirming the right of property, forgets that the owner is but a steward: the earth is the LORD's and the fulness thereof, and a man holds his goods in trust from God, accountable to use them justly, generously, and for the good of his neighbour. The dictionary holds the balance: property is a real and God-given right, to be defended against the thief and the collectivist alike; and it is a stewardship, to be held with an open hand under the lordship of the God who gave it.
webster_summary: The lawful right of ownership, grounded in the eighth commandment (Exodus 20:15), which presupposes that men rightly own what is theirs; a creational good, against collectivism that abolishes it and the greed that forgets the owner is a steward under God.

corruption_summary: Collectivism abolishes private property in the name of equality, violating the eighth commandment on a national scale; the opposite greed affirms the right but forgets the owner is a steward under God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right of property grounded in the eighth commandment. The first corruption is collectivism—the socialist and communist abolition of private property in the name of equality. The dictionary names it a violation of the eighth commandment on a national scale: the command “thou shalt not steal” presupposes lawful ownership, and a system that seizes what men rightly own breaks that command however it is dressed in the language of justice. Such collectivism breeds tyranny, for the state that owns all owns the men who depend on it. The early church's sharing in Acts was voluntary—the goods remaining the owners' to give, as Peter told Ananias—not a compelled communism.

The opposite corruption affirms the right of property but forgets that the owner is a steward. Greed and the idolatry of possessions treat what a man owns as absolutely his own, to hoard and consume for himself. But the earth is the LORD's and the fulness thereof; a man holds his goods in trust from God, accountable to use them justly, generously, and for the good of his neighbour. The dictionary holds both truths: private property is a real and God-given right, to be defended against the thief and the collectivist alike; and it is a stewardship, to be held with an open hand under the lordship of the God who gave it—owned truly, yet held loosely, and answered for at the last.

pos: noun phrase (the biblical doctrine of music)
etymology: From “music” (Greek mousike); the biblical treatment of music—its instruments, its place in worship and life, and its God-given power.
biblical_def: Music in the Bible is the whole biblical treatment of music—its instruments, its place in worship and in life, and its God-given power over the soul. Scripture is full of music. The Psalter calls for praise “with the sound of the trumpet… with the psaltery and harp… with the timbrel and dance… with stringed instruments and organs”; David appointed Levites as singers and players for the temple worship; and music attended the great moments of redemption—the song of Moses at the Red Sea, the songs of Zion, the new song of the redeemed in glory. The apostle bids the church sing “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.” The dictionary marks music as a good gift of God, given for His praise and for the gladdening of the human heart, with real power to move the affections—a power Scripture both honours (David's harp soothing Saul's troubled spirit) and treats soberly. It holds the biblical doctrine of music against opposite errors. The first is the asceticism that distrusts music as worldly or dangerous and would banish it—a denial of a gift God Himself commanded for His worship. The second is the modern abuse that makes music an end in itself, prizing performance, entertainment, and emotional manipulation over the truth sung and the God praised—letting the melody trample the words, or using music's power to work up feelings mistaken for the Spirit. In worship, music is governed by the regulative principle and the rule that it serve the word richly, the song teaching and admonishing in the truth. The dictionary commends music as a servant—of the praise of God and the good of the soul—neither despised as evil nor idolized as an end, but received as a gift and used to the glory of the Giver.
webster_summary: The biblical treatment of music—its instruments, its place in worship and life, and its God-given power (Psalm 150; Ephesians 5:19); a good gift for God's praise and the heart's gladness, against both ascetic distrust and the modern abuse that makes it an end in itself.

corruption_summary: One error is the asceticism that distrusts music as worldly and would banish it; the other is the modern abuse that makes music an end in itself, prizing performance and emotional manipulation over the truth sung.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is music as a good gift of God, servant of His praise and the soul's good. The first corruption is the asceticism that distrusts music as worldly or dangerous and would banish it from worship and life. The dictionary answers from the Psalter, which commands praise with trumpet, harp, timbrel, and strings, and from David, who appointed Levites to sing and play in the temple. Music is no enemy of godliness but a gift God Himself commanded for His worship, with power to gladden the heart and even, as David's harp soothed Saul, to quiet the troubled spirit.

The opposite and more modern corruption makes music an end in itself—prizing performance, entertainment, and emotional effect over the truth sung and the God praised. It lets the melody trample the words, fills worship with the vacant and the self-centred, and uses music's real power over the affections to work up feelings mistaken for the moving of the Spirit. The dictionary holds music to its proper place: a servant, not a master. In worship it is governed by the regulative principle and must serve the word richly, the song teaching and admonishing in the truth. Music is neither to be despised as evil nor idolized as an end, but received as a gift and used—in worship and in life—to the glory of the Giver.

etymology: Latin, “the art of dying”; the late-medieval body of devotional literature on how to die well, and, more broadly, the Christian discipline of preparing for death.
biblical_def: Ars moriendi, “the art of dying,” names the late-medieval body of devotional literature that taught Christians how to die well—to face death with faith, repentance, and hope—and, more broadly, the abiding Christian discipline of preparing for death. The medieval treatises, arising especially after the Black Death, counselled the dying against the temptations of unbelief, despair, impatience, pride, and avarice, and toward trust in Christ. The dictionary commends the recovery of the art of dying as a needful discipline for an age that hides death and refuses to prepare for it. Scripture commands such preparation: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom”; and it sets death in the light of judgment and hope—“it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment,” and yet, for the believer, “to die is gain.” The dying Paul could say, “the time of my departure is at hand,” with the peace of a finished course. The dictionary marks the art of dying against two errors. The medieval treatises themselves carried the corruptions of Rome—reliance on the last rites, penance, purgatory, and priestly absolution to secure the soul at death—and the dictionary refuses these, grounding the believer's hope in death not on sacraments administered but on Christ's finished work received by faith. The opposite, modern error is the denial of death altogether—the refusal to speak of it, prepare for it, or face it—leaving men to die unready and without hope. The dictionary recovers a Reformed art of dying: to number our days, to live ready, to repent and trust Christ, to set our house in order, and so to meet death not with the world's terror nor with Rome's false comforts, but with the assurance of the believer for whom to live is Christ and to die is gain.
webster_summary: “The art of dying”—the late-medieval literature and the abiding Christian discipline of preparing to die well (Psalm 90:12; Philippians 1:21); recovered in Reformed form, against Rome's last-rites reliance and the modern denial of death.

corruption_summary: The medieval treatises leaned on Rome's last rites, penance, and purgatory to secure the dying soul; the modern error denies death altogether, leaving men to die unready and without hope.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Christian preparation for death. The dictionary commends the discipline of the art of dying for an age that hides death and refuses to prepare for it. Scripture commands such preparation: teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom; and it bids the believer face death in the light of judgment and hope. To live ready to die is wisdom, not morbidity.

Two errors must be marked. The medieval treatises, for all their seriousness, carried the corruptions of Rome—leaning on the last rites, penance, purgatory, and priestly absolution to secure the soul at the hour of death. The dictionary refuses these false comforts, grounding the believer's hope in death not on sacraments administered by a priest but on Christ's finished work received by faith. The opposite, modern error is the denial of death—the refusal to speak of it, prepare for it, or face it—which leaves men to die unready and without hope. The dictionary recovers a Reformed art of dying: number your days, live ready, repent and trust Christ, set your house in order, and so meet death neither with the world's terror nor with Rome's false comforts, but with the assurance of the believer for whom to live is Christ and to die is gain.
